To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the Italian university system has been evaluated but not reformed; and that institutional accountability has been introduced in the system, but it has had little or no effect on the performance of the universities.
the Italian university system is in a condition of ‘evaluation without accountability’.

• Evaluation is not an end in itself, but a means to improve the quality of the system; • Evaluation is a necessary but insufficient tool for the improvement of the system; it must be combined with other instruments, such as the introduction of a more effective institutional accountability.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of whether the evaluation and accountability processes are really effective in steering universities in a more efficient direction.
the question of how evaluation has been introduced and managed in Italian higher education, and how the institutional and systemic governance arrangements have been affected.
the following question: why is the evaluation process in Italian higher education so ineffective?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the Italian university system is still in an early stage of the reform process and that it is not yet able to manage its own evaluation and accountability in a way that is consistent with the new governance arrangements.
the Italian case is an example of a Sisypheans task.
evaluation and institutional accountability in Italian universities have proved to be a Sisypheanic task.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

evaluation is a necessary but not sufficient condition for a successful reform of the Italian university system, which requires a more radical redefinition of the institutional and systemic governance arrangements.

the evaluation of university activities and institutional accountability are a Sisypheanic task in Italy, as in the other Western countries, but in our case it has proved to be more difficult and more frustrating than in the others.

the implementation of evaluation and institutional accountability has not been able to change the behaviour of universities in Italy, and has not been able either to produce a more efficient use of resources.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the Italian case is not an exceptional one, but it rather represents a typical case in a wider context where evaluation is a ‘Sisyphean task’.

the Italian university system has been unable to develop an evaluation process that is both effective and legitimate, and that it has been unable to implement an institutional accountability process capable of inducing the universities to behave responsibly.
the Italian case shows how the evaluation process and the accountability mechanisms are not able to produce the intended results.
